'''''Parietaria judaica''''', '''spreading pellitory''', is a species of [[herbaceous]] [[perennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Urticaceae]]. It is native to the eastern Mediterranean and Middle East, and is widely established worldwide as an urban weed. Its pollen is a significant cause of asthma and other allergies in warmer countries, but it is also valued as a contributor to biodiversity in polluted cities and it has been used as a medicinal herb.

==Description==
[[File:Urticaceae - Parietaria judaica.JPG|thumb|Close-up of a hermaphroditic flower before the stigma develops, showing the discharged anthers]] 
Spreading pellitory is a perennial [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] about 50 cm (up to 110 cm) tall with an upright to sprawling untidy habit. Plants can have many branched stems, which are pink or red and slightly woody and brittle at the base.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |publisher=C & M Floristics |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>
[[File:Parietaria judaica sl35.jpg|thumb|After pollination, the fruit begins to develop; here the red feathery stigmas can still be seen]]

The leaves are alternate, oval lanceolate, typically 3 cm long x 1.5 cm wide (exceptionally up to 6 cm x 3 cm) with a petiole about half as long as the blade. The veins on the lower side of the leaf are softly hairy, as are the leaf margins and the petiole. The upper surface is often glossy and either glabrous or with scattered hairs, and with sunken veins.<ref name=Poland>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |date=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>
[[File:Urticaceae - Parietaria judaica (2).JPG|thumb |Close-up of a leaf, showing venation and hairiness]]

Flowering can occur all year in suitable conditions in Europe.<ref name="Poland" /> The inflorescence consists of clusters in the leaf axils. Each cluster comprises 3-8 white or pink flowers, subtended by tiny bracts, of which typically one is [[Plant reproductive morphology#Unisexual|female-only]] and the other 2-7 are [[Plant reproductive morphology#Bisexual|hermaphroditic]] (although towards the eastern part of its range, the presence of female flowers is less common.<ref name="Townsend"/>) The female flower has 4 perianth segments (petals) and is 2 mm diameter (in fruit). The hermaphroditic flowers are tubular and up to 3 mm across (in fruit), with 4-5 stamens, which mature first, and one stigma, which develops later. When a hermaphroditic flower first opens, the [[stamen]]'s filaments are so elastic that they spring suddenly outward, dispersing the pollen ballistically from the anthers.<ref name=Grieve/><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Franchi |first=G.G. |last2=Nepi |first2=M. |last3=Matthews |first3=M.L. |last4=Pacini |first4=E. |date=2007 |title=Anther opening, pollen biology and stigma receptivity in the long blooming species ''Parietaria judaica'' L. (Urticaceae) |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/223183631_Anther_opening_pollen_biology_and_stigma_receptivity_in_the_long_blooming_species_Parietaria_judaica_L_Urticaceae |journal=Flora |volume=202 |issue=2 |pages=118-127 |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2006.03.005}}</ref>

The fruits are blackish [[achenes]] and often fall with the perianth, which has a proportion of minutely hooked hairs that produce the "stickiness" for which the plant is well-known.<ref name=Sell1>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland |volume=1 Lycopodiaceae — Salicaceae|date=2018 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-55335-3}}</ref>

==Identification==
Spreading pellitory is quite a distinctive plant. The species it is most likely to be confused with, where their ranges meet (e.g. in the eastern Mediterranean), is upright pellitory, ''[[Parietaria officinalis]]''. Under normal circumstances they should be fairly easy to separate, as upright pellitory has erect stems and large leaves (up to 12 cm, compared to less than 6 cm) but in intermediate plants the flower anatomy needs to be examined. Upright pellitory has a larger female flower (2.75 mm or more) than spreading pellitory (2.25 mm or less), and it is much longer than the bracts rather than about the same length.<ref name="Townsend">{{cite journal |last=Townsend |first=C.C. |year=1968 |url=http://www.watsonia.org.uk/Wats6p365.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726103016/http://www.watsonia.org.uk/Wats6p365.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=2011-07-26 |title=''Parietaria officinalis'' and ''P. judaica'' |journal=Watsonia |volume=6 |pages=6 }}</ref>
[[File:Urticaceae - Parietaria judaica-1.JPG|thumb|A length of stem with a cluster of flowers]]

==Taxonomy==
The scientific name for spreading pellitory was coined by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in the second edition of ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1763, based on his description of a specimen collected in Palestine by [[Fredrik Hasselqvist]] (hence the specific epithet ''judaica'' (Latin): of Judaea, Jewish).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Caroli Linnaei... Species plantarum: exhibentes plantas rite cognitas, ad genera relatas. |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/43462#page/709 |access-date=24 January 2024 |website=Biodiversity Heritage Library}}</ref> This is the name that is widely used now, although for a long time British plants were known as ''Parietaria diffusa'' <small>Mertens & Koch</small>.<ref name=Townsend /> The generic name ''Parietaria'' is derived from the Latin for "wall", ''paries'', via the adjective ''parietalis'' ("borne on the wall").<ref name=Stearn>{{cite book |last1=Stearn |first1=William T. |title=Botanical Latin: History, Grammar, Syntax, Terminology and Vocabulary |date=1980 |publisher=David & Charles |location=Newton Abbot |isbn=0-7153-5645-3}}</ref> The common name pellitory is most likely an [[Old French]] corruption of ''Parietaria''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Piretre |url=https://www.anglo-norman.net/entry/piretre |access-date=30 January 2024 |website=Anglo-Norman Dictionary}}</ref>

In ''Species Plantarum'' Linnaeus assigned it the [[Planet symbols|planet symbol]] for Jupiter (♃); This is simply a code to show that the plant is a perennial.<ref name="Stearn" />

There are no accepted subspecies or varieties of spreading pellitory; nor does it hybridise with any other species.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=''Parietaria judaica'' L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/102279519 |access-date=29 January 2024 |website=Global Biodiversity Information Forum}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2n = 26.<ref name="Stace" />

In England it is usually called "Pellitory-of-the-wall" (with the capital P and the hyphens) but elsewhere the less idiosyncratic name "spreading pellitory" is generally used, which contrasts well with "upright pellitory" for ''[[Parietaria officinalis]]''. Some popular sources give alternative nicknames "asthma weed" and '"sticky-weed" but it is, of course, not the only plant with these properties.<ref>[http://www.sydneyweeds.org.au/weeds/asthma-weed.php Sydney Weeds] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091116183250/http://www.sydneyweeds.org.au/weeds/asthma-weed.php |date=2009-11-16 }}</ref>

==Distribution and status==
[[File:Urticaceae - Parietaria judaica (1).JPG|thumb |A typical patch of spreading pellitory in flower]]
Spreading pellitory is a native of Macaronesia, N. Africa, Europe to Central Asia and Central Himalaya<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |work=Plants of the World Online |title=''Parietaria judaica'' L. |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Kew |access-date=23 January 2024 |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/854934-1 }}</ref><ref name=WeedsNSW>{{cite web |title=Pellitory (''Parietaria judaica'') |work=NSW WeedWise |publisher=NSW Department of Industry |url=http://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/Details/103 |access-date=2015-12-10 |archive-date=2017-12-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201032200/http://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/Details/103 |url-status=dead }}</ref> but has been introduced to parts of north and south Americas, Scandinavia and Australia.<ref name=POWO/>

The IUCN has not yet evaluated the global status of spreading pellitory, but in France, Britain and elsewhere it is considered unthreatened ("Least Concern", or LC), although in some regions it is rarer; for example, in [[Lorraine]] it is classified as endangered (EN) and it is absent from [[Alsace]] altogether.<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Parietaria judaica'' L. |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/112410?lg=fr |access-date=24 January 2024 |website=European Environment Agency}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel |title=Pariétaire de Judée, Pariétaire des murs, Pariétaire diffuse |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/112410 |access-date=24 January 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Cheffings |first1=C.M. | last2=Farrell |first2=L. |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |date=2005 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref>

It is a lowland plant, being recorded from sea level up to about 125 m in California<ref>{{Cite web |title=Parietaria judaica |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=36254#:~:text=Flower%3A%20calyx%20lobes%202%2D%2D,native%20to%20Eurasia%2C%20northern%20Africa. |access-date=31 January 2024 |website=Jepson eFlora}}</ref> and no higher than 200 m anywhere in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Parietaria judaica |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Parietaria_judaica |access-date=31 January 2024 |website=Flora of North America}}</ref> Altitudinal data for it is not collected in Britain, but analysis of the regions where it grows shows no land above 500 m and very little over 300 m.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pellitory-of-the-wall ''Parietaria judaica'' L. In Portugal, though, it has been recorded almost up to 1000m high (Flora on.pt). |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.vq4 |access-date=31 January 2024 |website=Plant Atlas 2020}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
[[File:Parietaria judaica in Lebanon.jpg|thumb|A patch of spreading pellitory in its native habitat in Lebanon]]
In its native habitat, spreading pellitory grows on rocks and bare ground in slightly damp and sheltered places such as seasonal river valleys in limestone areas of the Eastern Mediterranean. It is, however, well adapted to synanthropic habitats in towns, where it can exploit the [[urban heat island]] effect to thrive in colder climates. It has also become common in other continents, where it can benefit by competitive release from its pests and predators.

[[File:Parietaria judaica habitus on wall 2.jpg|thumb|Spreading pellitory often grows from the gaps between bricks in a wall]]
In an urban landscape its main habitat is at the base of walls, where there is increased dampness, light shade and protection from trampling. It grows on bare soil or in the gap at the edge of the pavement and it is tolerant of light salinity, so it can occur in coastal towns and beside roads that are treated with salt. Plants are also found in gaps in the mortar between bricks or stones of older or damp walls, on shingle, and at the bottom of hedges. Plant density is highest in old town centres, thinning out in the suburbs until it becomes virtually absent from the open countryside. This is presumably because it is highly palatable to livestock.<ref name="Mabey" /> It grows in conditions that few other plants can tolerate and, as a consequence, it is found in very species-poor communities, often with no other associates whatsoever.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dana |first=E.D. |last2=Vivas |first2=S. |last3=Mota |first3=J.F. |date=2002 |title=Urban vegetation of Almerı́a City—a contribution to urban ecology in Spain |journal=Landscape and Urban Planning |volume=59 |issue=4 |pages=203-216 |doi=10.1016/S0169-2046(02)00039-7 |via=Science Direct}}</ref>

In sheltered places, spreading pellitory is an evergreen plant which typically produces smaller leaves to survive the winter (in the north) or the summer months (in warmer countries), or it dies back to a dense tangle of woody stems in less hospitable spots. It can be found in flower at any time of year, but the main flowering seasons are the autumn and spring in the Mediterranean region, or summer in northern Europe. Flowering is strongly influenced by aspect (south-facing walls in the northern hemisphere), temperature (best in warmer countries) and [[climate change]] (increased flowering in a warming environment).<ref name=Fotiou>{{Cite journal |last=Fotiou |first=Christina |last2=Damialis |first2=Athanasios |last3=Krigas |first3=Nikolaos |last4=Halley |first4=John M. |last5=Vokou |first5=Despoina |date=2010 |title=''Parietaria judaica'' flowering phenology, pollen production, viability and atmospheric circulation, and expansive ability in the urban environment: impacts of environmental factors |journal=Int. J. Biometeorol. |volume=55 |pages=35-50 |doi=10.1007/s00484-010-0307-3}}</ref>

The [[British National Vegetation Classification]] gives ''Parietaria diffusa'' (i.e. ''P. judaica'') its own [[Phytosociology|phytosociological]] community, OV41, which occurs on walls or coastal cliffs. The OV41a wall community is rather species-poor, with typically only about 7 other plants present in a sample, most commonly the mosses ''[[Homalothecium sericeum]]'' and ''[[Tortula muralis]]''. The OV41b coastal community, however, has an average of 17 species per sample, including [[Festuca rubra|red fescue]] and [[Daucus carota|wild carrot]]. It can also contain several rare species such as [[Brassica oleracea|wild cabbage]].<ref name=Rodwell5>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vol. 5: Maritime communities and vegetation of open habitats|year=2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

In continental Europe, the ''Parietanetalia'' community of old city walls is considered an important refuge for endangered species.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brandes |first=Dietmar |date=1992 |title=Flora und Vegetation von Stadtmauern |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/236973401_Flora_und_Vegetation_von_Stadtmauern |journal=Tuexenia |volume=12 |pages=315-339}}</ref>

Spreading pellitory is tolerant of the high levels of heavy metal pollution caused by traffic in the urban environment. Metals such as [[lead]], [[cadmium]], [[copper]] and [[zinc]] accumulate within its tissues,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Aksoy |first=A. |last2=Osma |first2=E. |last3=Leblebici |first3=Z. |date=2012 |title=Spreading Pellitory (''Parietaria judaica'' L.): a possible biomonitor of heavy metal pollution |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/236502638 |journal=Pakistan Journal of Botany |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=123-127}}</ref> and have been shown to cause increased pollen production.<ref name="Fotiou" />

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in central Europe are L = 6, F = 7, R = 8, N = 7, and S = 1, which show that it favours damp, reasonably sunny places on slightly alkaline soils and rich fertility, and that it can occur in slightly brackish situations.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref>

This species is wind pollinated.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://pfaf.org/USER/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Parietaria+judaica |publisher=Plants for a Future |title=''Parietaria judaica''}}</ref> Seeds are adhesive and transported by insects as well as other animals, people and machines.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=3471  |title=''Parietaria judaica'' |publisher=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network}}</ref>

The larvae of the red admiral butterfly (''[[Vanessa atalanta]]'') and the Bloxworth snout moth (''[[Hypena obsitalis]]'') feed on pellitories, including spreading pelltiory,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Parietaria judaica |url=https://dbif.brc.ac.uk/hostsresults.aspx?hostid=3829 |access-date=16 January 2024 |website=Database of Insects and their Food Plants}}</ref> as do several species of aphid, most notably ''Aphis parietariae''.<ref name=Crawley>{{cite book |last1=Crawley |first1=M.J. |title=The Flora of Berkshire |date=2005 |publisher=Brambleby Books |location=Harpenden |isbn=0-9543347-4-4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Aphis parietariae |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/parasites/animalia/arthropoda/insecta/hemiptera/sternorrhyncha/aphidoidea/aphididae/aphidinae/aphidini/aphis/aphis-parietariae/ |access-date=24 January 2024 |website=Plant Parasites of Europe}}</ref>

==Uses and effects==
The pollen of spreading pellitory is one of the leading causes of respiratory allergies ([[asthma]] and [[rhinitis]]) in the Mediterranean region, particularly at peak flowering times in the spring and autumn.<ref name=stumvoll>{{cite journal |vauthors=Stumvoll S, Westritschnig K, Lidholm J, Spitzauer S, Colombo P, Duro G, Kraft D, Geraci D, Valenta R |title=Identification of cross-reactive and genuine ''Parietaria judaica'' pollen allergens |journal=J. Allergy Clin. Immunol. |volume=111 |issue=5 |pages=974–9 |date=May 2003 |pmid=12743560 |doi=10.1067/mai.2003.1376 |doi-access=free }}</ref> One study estimated that the huge population of pellitory in a city in Greece could produce as many as 5.4 billion pollen grains per square metre during the spring months, causing many medical problems.<ref name="Fotiou" />

It has been established in Australia since 1902 or earlier, especially in Sydney, Melbourne and Fremantle, where it is considered a noxious weed. Control is effected by the application of [[glyphosate]], although it can grow back quickly from the persistent soil seed bank.<ref>{{Cite conference |last1=Bass |first1=D.A. |last2=Clements |first2=A. |date=1990 |title=Biology and control of ''Parietaria judaica'' L., an ellergenic weed in south-eastern Australia |book-title=Proceedings of the Ninth Australian Weed Conference, Adelaide, South Australia, August 6-10, 1990 |pages=516–520 |oclc=154211543 |url=https://www.cabdirect.org/cabdirect/abstract/19922318249}}</ref>

In herbal medicine it was supposed to be efficacious against kidney and bladder stones, presumably because its roots appear to be splitting stone walls.<ref name=Mabey>{{cite book |last1=Mabey |first1=Richard |title=Flora Britannica |date=1996 |publisher=Reed International |isbn=1-85619-377-2}}</ref> The celebrated herbalist of the early 20th century  [[Maud Grieve]] considered that its "action upon the urinary calculus is perhaps more marked than any other simple agent at present employed".<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book |last1=Grieve |first1=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |date=1931 |publisher=Dover  |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref> Some [[Romani people]] apparently use it to treat sores, ulcers and piles.<ref>{{cite book|title=Hatfield's Herbal: The Curious Stories of Britain's Wild Plants}}</ref>

Some authors consider that the plant listed by the Ancient Greek herbalist [[Pedanius Dioscorides|Dioscorides]] as ''Helxine'' is spreading pellitory. The description seems quite apt: "helxine grows in mounds and walls. It has thin little stalks, somewhat red, rough leaves similar to [[Mercurialis annua|mercury]]; and around the stalks (as it were) sharp little seeds, catching hold of cloths." He considered it to be useful against all type of inflammation, oedema, and for many other purposes. Fifteen hundred years later the English herbalist [[Nicholas Culpeper]] gave a similar description but with the introduction of some errors such as opposite leaves, and considered it a useful antidiuretic and general cure-all.<ref name=Dioscorides>{{cite web | vauthors = Dioscorides P | author-link = Pedanius Dioscorides | title = De Materia Medica | url = https://ia802907.us.archiveclarke.org/16/items/de-materia-medica/scribd-download.com_dioscorides-de-materia-medica.pdf }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Culpeper |first1=Nicholas |title=The Complete Herbal |date=1850 |publisher=Thomas Kelly |location=London |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513}}</ref>
